The *Daṇḍa Sutta* (Ud 2.3; PTS Ud 11) is a short discourse in the *Udāna* collection of the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral]. In this text, the Buddha imparts a moral lesson directed toward young boys, instructing that anyone who desires happiness and seeks to avoid suffering should refrain from inflicting violence or pain upon other living beings [SuttaCentral]. SuttaCentral lists 16 modern translations in 13 languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato, and records references to the sutta in the paracanonical *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 9 and Ne 37) [SuttaCentral].

The verse material of the sutta possesses widespread parallels across early Buddhist literature and the broader Indian textual tradition [SuttaCentral]. In the Pali Canon, passage-level parallels are found in the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 131–132, in the *Daṇḍavagga*); corresponding verses are attested in the Patna Dharmapada (P-Dhp 195–215), the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (UV 30, *Sukhavarga*), the Tibetan translation (*Uv Kg* 30), and multiple Chinese translations, including T 210 (chapter 18), T 212 (chapter 31), and T 213 (chapter 30) [SuttaCentral]. Outside Buddhist literature, related verses occur in the *Mahābhārata* (13.114.005) and the *Manusmṛti* (5.45) [SuttaCentral]. Within the Pali corpus, DharmaNexus identifies substantial textual reuse, sharing its narrative framework and verses most closely with the *Kumāraka Sutta* (Ud 5.4, §1.1–1.5 matching §1.1–2.2 with 0.95 similarity), as well as standard formulaic phrasing shared with the *Māra Saṁyutta* (SN 4), *Devatā Saṁyutta* (SN 1), *Aṅgulimāla Sutta* (MN 86), and *Mahārāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 62) [DharmaNexus].
